case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.
case_info.caption: A, Left dorsal hand with a 1-cm shiny red, firm exophytic nodule with a scaling collarette at the base. B, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×400) of left forearm lesion biopsy shows clumps of basophilic material in the stroma and a superficial area of ulceration with lobular proliferation of vessels and central necrosis infiltrated by neutrophils. Fibrotic stroma with neutrophilic infiltration and red cell extravasation.
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a benign vascular proliferation and neutrophilic aggregate with positive Warthin-Starry stain suggestive of bacillary angiomatosis (Figure 2). Whole blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) forBartonellaspecies was positive with positive serologic IgG (1:256) and negative IgMB quintanaantibodies and equivocalB henselaeIgG (1:64) with IgM negativity, confirming bacillary angiomatosis. Bacillary peliosis, characterized by blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver and spleen, was found on magnetic resonance imaging. An infectious disease physician prescribed doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, for 3 months. Gastrointestinal symptoms resulted in self-discontinuation of treatment, despite the persistent hand lesion. Complete resolution occurred with a course of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, for 2 months. Bacillary angiomatosis is a disseminated disease caused by the small, pleomorphic, gram-negative rod,B henselaeorB quintana,most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and patients with advanced HIV disease.1,2Bacillary angiomatosis has been reported infrequently in adult solid organ transplant recipients with most presenting months after transplant, unlike the present patient presenting 11 years posttransplant.2Transmission occurs by direct contact with cats via scratches, fleas, or human body lice. Skin is most frequently involved, followed by bones and liver, and presents as single or multiple erythematous or violaceous papules or nodules.1,2Patients often experience constitutional symptoms of fever, anorexia, and weight loss.2 The diagnosis of cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis can be challenging, often requiring multiple diagnostic modalities, including skin biopsy and PCR.Bartonella, a fastidious organism, is difficult to isolate via culture and with a 20% sensitivity.3Serology can be useful in combination with whole blood PCR, but difficult to interpret due to high rates of cross-reactivity betweenBartonellaspecies.3TheBartonellaspecies could not be determined in this case due to serologic cross-reactivity, but genus-level identification guided effective treatment, which is similar across species. Tissue biopsy with PCR is a specific method for identification ofBartonellaspecies, making this molecular test crucial to diagnose cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis.4Histopathology is notable for neutrophilic infiltration and collections of organisms, identified with a Warthin-Starry stain.5Advanced imaging is necessary to exclude peliosis and to guide management in preventing complications such as liver failure and potential rupture.6 The differential diagnosis for bacillary angiomatosis includes Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma, pyogenic granuloma, and mycobacterial and fungal infections. While Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV infection, iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma has been reported in patients on immunosuppressive therapies and in transplant recipients. Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma presents as painless, well-defined, pink to purple patches, plaques, or nodules.7Kaposi sarcoma can be distinguished histopathologically from bacillary angiomatosis by spindle cell vascular proliferation in the dermis and immunohistochemistry staining positive for latent nuclear antigen-1 (LNA-1), a marker for human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8).8Pyogenic granulomas are extremely friable, benign vascular lesions that rapidly develop as a single red papule or polyp.5Pyogenic granulomas can share overlapping features with bacillary angiomatosis but have a lobular appearance and lack the clusters of neutrophils seen in bacillary angiomatosis.9Advanced angiosarcoma lesions can resemble bacillary angiomatosis with violaceous nodules that easily bleed. Histopathology reveals ill-defined vascular spaces with multilayering of hyperchromatic endothelial cells.5 Recommended treatment for bacillary angiomatosis includes erythromycin, 500 mg, 4 times daily or doxycycline, 100 mg, twice daily for 2 weeks to 2 months.10Longer therapy duration of at least 3 months may be necessary in immunocompromised states.2Preventive measures include eradication of body lice and strict flea-control measures for cats.1 Bacillary angiomatosis is critical to recognize in immunocompromised patients. Clinically, these lesions may appear similar to malignant and benign entities, making histopathology and laboratory testing essential for accurate diagnosis. It is critical to use multiple diagnostic modalities, including biopsy with Warthin-Starry stain, serology, and PCR testing. Comprehensive workup, including advanced imaging to exclude systemic involvement, is warranted to prevent potentially fatal outcomes.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.

  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Left dorsal hand with a 1-cm shiny red, firm exophytic nodule with a scaling collarette at the base. B, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×400) of left forearm lesion biopsy shows clumps of basophilic material in the stroma and a superficial area of ulceration with lobular proliferation of vessels and central necrosis infiltrated by neutrophils. case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a benign vascular proliferation and neutrophilic aggregate with positive Warthin-Starry stain suggestive of bacillary angiomatosis (Figure 2). Whole blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) forBartonellaspecies was positive with positive serologic IgG (1:256) and negative IgMB quintanaantibodies and equivocalB henselaeIgG (1:64) with IgM negativity, confirming bacillary angiomatosis. Bacillary peliosis, characterized by blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver and spleen, was found on magnetic resonance imaging. An infectious disease physician prescribed doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, for 3 months. Gastrointestinal symptoms resulted in self-discontinuation of treatment, despite the persistent hand lesion. Complete resolution occurred with a course of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, for 2 months. Bacillary angiomatosis is a disseminated disease caused by the small, pleomorphic, gram-negative rod,B henselaeorB quintana,most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and patients with advanced HIV disease.1,2Bacillary angiomatosis has been reported infrequently in adult solid organ transplant recipients with most presenting months after transplant, unlike the present patient presenting 11 years posttransplant.2Transmission occurs by direct contact with cats via scratches, fleas, or human body lice. Skin is most frequently involved, followed by bones and liver, and presents as single or multiple erythematous or violaceous papules or nodules.1,2Patients often experience constitutional symptoms of fever, anorexia, and weight loss.2 The diagnosis of cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis can be challenging, often requiring multiple diagnostic modalities, including skin biopsy and PCR.Bartonella, a fastidious organism, is difficult to isolate via culture and with a 20% sensitivity.3Serology can be useful in combination with whole blood PCR, but difficult to interpret due to high rates of cross-reactivity betweenBartonellaspecies.3TheBartonellaspecies could not be determined in this case due to serologic cross-reactivity, but genus-level identification guided effective treatment, which is similar across species. Tissue biopsy with PCR is a specific method for identification ofBartonellaspecies, making this molecular test crucial to diagnose cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis.4Histopathology is notable for neutrophilic infiltration and collections of organisms, identified with a Warthin-Starry stain.5Advanced imaging is necessary to exclude peliosis and to guide management in preventing complications such as liver failure and potential rupture.6 The differential diagnosis for bacillary angiomatosis includes Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma, pyogenic granuloma, and mycobacterial and fungal infections. While Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV infection, iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma has been reported in patients on immunosuppressive therapies and in transplant recipients. Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma presents as painless, well-defined, pink to purple patches, plaques, or nodules.7Kaposi sarcoma can be distinguished histopathologically from bacillary angiomatosis by spindle cell vascular proliferation in the dermis and immunohistochemistry staining positive for latent nuclear antigen-1 (LNA-1), a marker for human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8).8Pyogenic granulomas are extremely friable, benign vascular lesions that rapidly develop as a single red papule or polyp.5Pyogenic granulomas can share overlapping features with bacillary angiomatosis but have a lobular appearance and lack the clusters of neutrophils seen in bacillary angiomatosis.9Advanced angiosarcoma lesions can resemble bacillary angiomatosis with violaceous nodules that easily bleed. Histopathology reveals ill-defined vascular spaces with multilayering of hyperchromatic endothelial cells.5 Recommended treatment for bacillary angiomatosis includes erythromycin, 500 mg, 4 times daily or doxycycline, 100 mg, twice daily for 2 weeks to 2 months.10Longer therapy duration of at least 3 months may be necessary in immunocompromised states.2Preventive measures include eradication of body lice and strict flea-control measures for cats.1 Bacillary angiomatosis is critical to recognize in immunocompromised patients. Clinically, these lesions may appear similar to malignant and benign entities, making histopathology and laboratory testing essential for accurate diagnosis. It is critical to use multiple diagnostic modalities, including biopsy with Warthin-Starry stain, serology, and PCR testing. Comprehensive workup, including advanced imaging to exclude systemic involvement, is warranted to prevent potentially fatal outcomes.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Currently reachable stages (Hitchcock ordering rules): CONSIDER, INFORM, PROPOSE, RECOMMEND
You MUST pick a stage from this list.

Further specific tests for Bartonella species would help confirm the diagnosis.

The histological description of lobular proliferation of vessels without high-grade atypia is characteristic of bacillary angiomatosis, whereas Kaposi sarcoma shows spindle cells and angiosarcoma shows malignant endothelial cells. Negative tissue cultures for common pathogens do not rule out Bartonella, which requires specific tests.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Stage: INFORM | Locution: ask_justify(fact)
Apply this deliberation move in your response.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the clinical presentation of multiple painless, firm, red papules with ulceration, fever, night sweats, and the patient's immunocompromised state due to transplant medication, the most appropriate next step in management is to suspect bacillary angiomatosis. This condition is often associated with immunosuppression and can mimic other vascular lesions. The history of frequent exposure to cats raises the likelihood of this diagnosis, particularly when coupled with the patient's symptoms and skin findings. Therefore, further investigation looking for Bartonella species would be warranted.

That's a reasonable suspicion given the cat exposure and immunosuppression. Can you clarify why you think bacillary angiomatosis is more likely than, say, Kaposi sarcoma or other vascular neoplasms in this setting? What specific findings from the skin biopsy or imaging would help justify that focus?

[Clinician's current statement]

The biopsy showing lobular proliferation of vessels also aligns more with bacillary angiomatosis than with malignancies like Kaposi sarcoma or angiosarcoma, which would typically show more atypical cellular features. Further specific tests for Bartonella species would help confirm the diagnosis.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it
    deterministically from your 4 integer scores>,
  "short_rationale": {
    "mental_demand": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "performance": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "effort": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "frustration": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>"
  }
}

[Clinical case]

case_info.caption: A, Left dorsal hand with a 1-cm shiny red, firm exophytic nodule with a scaling collarette at the base. B, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×400) of left forearm lesion biopsy shows clumps of basophilic material in the stroma and a superficial area of ulceration with lobular proliferation of vessels and central necrosis infiltrated by neutrophils. case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a benign vascular proliferation and neutrophilic aggregate with positive Warthin-Starry stain suggestive of bacillary angiomatosis (Figure 2). Whole blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) forBartonellaspecies was positive with positive serologic IgG (1:256) and negative IgMB quintanaantibodies and equivocalB henselaeIgG (1:64) with IgM negativity, confirming bacillary angiomatosis. Bacillary peliosis, characterized by blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver and spleen, was found on magnetic resonance imaging. An infectious disease physician prescribed doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, for 3 months. Gastrointestinal symptoms resulted in self-discontinuation of treatment, despite the persistent hand lesion. Complete resolution occurred with a course of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, for 2 months. Bacillary angiomatosis is a disseminated disease caused by the small, pleomorphic, gram-negative rod,B henselaeorB quintana,most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and patients with advanced HIV disease.1,2Bacillary angiomatosis has been reported infrequently in adult solid organ transplant recipients with most presenting months after transplant, unlike the present patient presenting 11 years posttransplant.2Transmission occurs by direct contact with cats via scratches, fleas, or human body lice. Skin is most frequently involved, followed by bones and liver, and presents as single or multiple erythematous or violaceous papules or nodules.1,2Patients often experience constitutional symptoms of fever, anorexia, and weight loss.2 The diagnosis of cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis can be challenging, often requiring multiple diagnostic modalities, including skin biopsy and PCR.Bartonella, a fastidious organism, is difficult to isolate via culture and with a 20% sensitivity.3Serology can be useful in combination with whole blood PCR, but difficult to interpret due to high rates of cross-reactivity betweenBartonellaspecies.3TheBartonellaspecies could not be determined in this case due to serologic cross-reactivity, but genus-level identification guided effective treatment, which is similar across species. Tissue biopsy with PCR is a specific method for identification ofBartonellaspecies, making this molecular test crucial to diagnose cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis.4Histopathology is notable for neutrophilic infiltration and collections of organisms, identified with a Warthin-Starry stain.5Advanced imaging is necessary to exclude peliosis and to guide management in preventing complications such as liver failure and potential rupture.6 The differential diagnosis for bacillary angiomatosis includes Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma, pyogenic granuloma, and mycobacterial and fungal infections. While Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV infection, iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma has been reported in patients on immunosuppressive therapies and in transplant recipients. Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma presents as painless, well-defined, pink to purple patches, plaques, or nodules.7Kaposi sarcoma can be distinguished histopathologically from bacillary angiomatosis by spindle cell vascular proliferation in the dermis and immunohistochemistry staining positive for latent nuclear antigen-1 (LNA-1), a marker for human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8).8Pyogenic granulomas are extremely friable, benign vascular lesions that rapidly develop as a single red papule or polyp.5Pyogenic granulomas can share overlapping features with bacillary angiomatosis but have a lobular appearance and lack the clusters of neutrophils seen in bacillary angiomatosis.9Advanced angiosarcoma lesions can resemble bacillary angiomatosis with violaceous nodules that easily bleed. Histopathology reveals ill-defined vascular spaces with multilayering of hyperchromatic endothelial cells.5 Recommended treatment for bacillary angiomatosis includes erythromycin, 500 mg, 4 times daily or doxycycline, 100 mg, twice daily for 2 weeks to 2 months.10Longer therapy duration of at least 3 months may be necessary in immunocompromised states.2Preventive measures include eradication of body lice and strict flea-control measures for cats.1 Bacillary angiomatosis is critical to recognize in immunocompromised patients. Clinically, these lesions may appear similar to malignant and benign entities, making histopathology and laboratory testing essential for accurate diagnosis. It is critical to use multiple diagnostic modalities, including biopsy with Warthin-Starry stain, serology, and PCR testing. Comprehensive workup, including advanced imaging to exclude systemic involvement, is warranted to prevent potentially fatal outcomes.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Left dorsal hand with a 1-cm shiny red, firm exophytic nodule with a scaling collarette at the base. case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a benign vascular proliferation and neutrophilic aggregate with positive Warthin-Starry stain suggestive of bacillary angiomatosis (Figure 2). Whole blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) forBartonellaspecies was positive with positive serologic IgG (1:256) and negative IgMB quintanaantibodies and equivocalB henselaeIgG (1:64) with IgM negativity, confirming bacillary angiomatosis. Bacillary peliosis, characterized by blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver and spleen, was found on magnetic resonance imaging. An infectious disease physician prescribed doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, for 3 months. Gastrointestinal symptoms resulted in self-discontinuation of treatment, despite the persistent hand lesion. Complete resolution occurred with a course of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, for 2 months. Bacillary angiomatosis is a disseminated disease caused by the small, pleomorphic, gram-negative rod,B henselaeorB quintana,most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and patients with advanced HIV disease.1,2Bacillary angiomatosis has been reported infrequently in adult solid organ transplant recipients with most presenting months after transplant, unlike the present patient presenting 11 years posttransplant.2Transmission occurs by direct contact with cats via scratches, fleas, or human body lice. Skin is most frequently involved, followed by bones and liver, and presents as single or multiple erythematous or violaceous papules or nodules.1,2Patients often experience constitutional symptoms of fever, anorexia, and weight loss.2 The diagnosis of cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis can be challenging, often requiring multiple diagnostic modalities, including skin biopsy and PCR.Bartonella, a fastidious organism, is difficult to isolate via culture and with a 20% sensitivity.3Serology can be useful in combination with whole blood PCR, but difficult to interpret due to high rates of cross-reactivity betweenBartonellaspecies.3TheBartonellaspecies could not be determined in this case due to serologic cross-reactivity, but genus-level identification guided effective treatment, which is similar across species. Tissue biopsy with PCR is a specific method for identification ofBartonellaspecies, making this molecular test crucial to diagnose cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis.4Histopathology is notable for neutrophilic infiltration and collections of organisms, identified with a Warthin-Starry stain.5Advanced imaging is necessary to exclude peliosis and to guide management in preventing complications such as liver failure and potential rupture.6 The differential diagnosis for bacillary angiomatosis includes Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma, pyogenic granuloma, and mycobacterial and fungal infections. While Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV infection, iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma has been reported in patients on immunosuppressive therapies and in transplant recipients. Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma presents as painless, well-defined, pink to purple patches, plaques, or nodules.7Kaposi sarcoma can be distinguished histopathologically from bacillary angiomatosis by spindle cell vascular proliferation in the dermis and immunohistochemistry staining positive for latent nuclear antigen-1 (LNA-1), a marker for human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8).8Pyogenic granulomas are extremely friable, benign vascular lesions that rapidly develop as a single red papule or polyp.5Pyogenic granulomas can share overlapping features with bacillary angiomatosis but have a lobular appearance and lack the clusters of neutrophils seen in bacillary angiomatosis.9Advanced angiosarcoma lesions can resemble bacillary angiomatosis with violaceous nodules that easily bleed. Histopathology reveals ill-defined vascular spaces with multilayering of hyperchromatic endothelial cells.5 Recommended treatment for bacillary angiomatosis includes erythromycin, 500 mg, 4 times daily or doxycycline, 100 mg, twice daily for 2 weeks to 2 months.10Longer therapy duration of at least 3 months may be necessary in immunocompromised states.2Preventive measures include eradication of body lice and strict flea-control measures for cats.1 Bacillary angiomatosis is critical to recognize in immunocompromised patients. Clinically, these lesions may appear similar to malignant and benign entities, making histopathology and laboratory testing essential for accurate diagnosis. It is critical to use multiple diagnostic modalities, including biopsy with Warthin-Starry stain, serology, and PCR testing. Comprehensive workup, including advanced imaging to exclude systemic involvement, is warranted to prevent potentially fatal outcomes.
